name: Battle of the Plains of Abraham
info: British troops under James Wolfe defeated French regulars and Canadian militia under the Marquis de Montcalm outside Quebec City on 13 September 1759, during the Seven Years' War; the city capitulated five days later.

facts.place: The Plains of Abraham, a plateau on the Promontory of Quebec just outside the walls of Quebec City, in the colony of Canada, New France, now in Quebec, Canada
facts.sides: Britain under Major General James Wolfe, with 4,426 men by the Government of Canada's figures (from André Charbonneau) or about 7,700 by another count; France and Canada under the Marquis de Montcalm, with 2,000 French Army troops, 600 Canadians drafted into regular units and 1,800 militiamen and Indian allies by the same Canadian figures
facts.outcome: The French were driven from the field in about an hour. Both generals were mortally wounded, and Quebec capitulated on 18 September.

t: Strengths are given differently by different counts: 4,426 British soldiers by one Canadian government figure, about 7,700 by another count, and 13,390 French troops available in the area, most of whom did not take part.
The British held their fire until the French column was within about 30 yards (27 m), then fired two heavy volleys, and the attack broke in about an hour.
Wolfe and Montcalm both died of their wounds, and France lost Canada in the Treaty of Paris of 1763 after the fall of Montreal in 1760.
dyk: Wolfe's troops climbed to the plateau at L'Anse-au-Foulon after a French-speaking officer of the 78th Highlanders answered a sentry's challenge in excellent French, and it is not known why Wolfe chose that landing place.
ev: Wolfe lands on the Île d'Orléans and then at Point Levis, opposite Quebec
About 3,500 British troops fail to land at Beauport and Wolfe withdraws after some 450 casualties
British troops land at L'Anse-au-Foulon at night and climb to the plateau
The British line stops the French advance outside Quebec, and Wolfe and Montcalm are mortally wounded
Quebec capitulates and the British take the city
Lévis defeats the British at Sainte-Foy but cannot take Quebec
The Treaty of Paris cedes Canada to Britain

sections.background:
In 1759 the British prepared a three-pronged attack on New France. James Wolfe expected to lead 12,000 men but had about 7,000 regular troops, 400 officers and 300 gunners, supported by 49 ships and 140 smaller craft under Vice-Admiral Charles Saunders. He landed on the Île d'Orléans on 28 June, after James Cook had surveyed the channel known as the Traverse, and on the next day his troops landed at Point Levis, where a battery set up in early July nearly levelled the lower town.

Montcalm distributed some 12,000 troops along nine kilometres of redoubts and batteries from the Saint-Charles River to the Montmorency Falls. On 31 July about 3,500 British troops tried to land at Beauport and were fired on in the shallows; Wolfe pulled back after some 450 casualties to Montcalm's 60. For the rest of the summer his troops, with American Rangers, destroyed small French settlements along the St. Lawrence, an estimated 1,400 stone houses and manors, and many colonists were killed. The effort was probably meant to force Montcalm out of his fortifications, and failed.

Illness spread through the British camps, and Wolfe, bedridden in August, felt that a new attack was needed by the end of September. In late August he and his brigadiers decided to land upriver of the city, which would cut Montcalm's supply lines to Montreal.
sections.forces:
The British were commanded by Major General James Wolfe, and the numbers vary by source. The Government of Canada's website, using the historian André Charbonneau's figures, gives 4,426 British Army soldiers on the Plains with two bronze 6-pounder cannon. Another count has 7,700 troops, almost all regulars, of whom about 3,300 formed a shallow horseshoe across the Plains, the main firing line roughly one kilometre long. To cover the width Wolfe drew them up two ranks deep rather than three. The Louisbourg Grenadiers and the 28th, 43rd, 47th, 58th and 78th (Fraser's Highlanders) held the centre, the 15th and two battalions of the 60th the left, the 35th the right flank, the 48th the reserve.

The French under Louis-Joseph, Marquis de Montcalm were regulars, militia and Indian allies. Charbonneau's figures are 2,000 men of the French Army, 600 Canadians drafted into regular units and 1,800 militiamen and Indian allies; the French had more cannon, but their number is not known. Another count has 13,390 regulars, Troupes de la Marine and militia available in Quebec City and along the Beauport shore, most of whom did not take part, and about 3,500 soldiers in the attack. The militia were poorly armed with rifles and no bayonets, and the Indian allies were unfamiliar with European tactics. Montcalm placed militia on the right, the La Sarre, Languedoc and Béarn regiments in the centre, and the Guyenne and Royal Roussillon regiments with Montréal and Trois-Rivières militia on the left.
sections.course:
On the night of 12 September the British landed at L'Anse-au-Foulon, below a cliff 53 m high. Sentries challenged the boats, but a French-speaking officer of the 78th answered in excellent French, and the boats had drifted off course. Twenty-four volunteers under Colonel William Howe climbed the slope and captured the camp of about 100 militia under Captain Vergor, which may have held as few as 40 men. Montcalm, surprised, chose to confront Wolfe directly rather than wait for Bougainville's column.

The French advanced at about 10 a.m., Montcalm riding a dark horse and waving his sword. The British held their fire until the French were within 30 yards (27 m), and the two armies waited two or three minutes. The French fired two disorganised volleys. The British, who had charged their muskets with two balls each, fired a heavy volley, advanced a few paces and fired a second that sent the attackers into retreat. Wolfe, already struck in the wrist, was hit twice and died as the French broke. The 78th Highlanders pursued with swords and took the highest casualties of any British unit. Townshend turned two battalions on Bougainville's column, arriving from Cap Rouge, and Bougainville retreated. Montcalm, wounded in the lower abdomen and thigh during the retreat, reached the city and died early the next morning.
sections.aftermath:
British casualties were 658 killed or wounded, of them 61 killed and 597 wounded. French casualties were between 644 and 716 killed or wounded, thirteen of them officers, and a further 350 men were taken prisoner. Montcalm was buried in a crater left in the floor of the Ursuline chapel by a British shell.

Governor de Vaudreuil, who later put the full blame for the rout on Montcalm, abandoned Quebec and the Beauport shore and ordered his forces west to join Bougainville, leaving de Ramezay in command of the garrison. On 18 September de Ramezay, Townshend and Saunders signed the Articles of Capitulation of Quebec. The British navy had to leave the St. Lawrence soon after, before pack ice closed its mouth.

In April 1760 Lévis, Montcalm's successor, marched 7,000 troops on Quebec, where scurvy had reduced Murray's garrison to 4,000. On 28 April the French won at Sainte-Foy, with about 850 casualties against 1,100 British, but the British withdrew within the walls and the French lacked the artillery and ammunition to storm them. A British fleet that arrived in mid-May had defeated Lévis' support ships, and at Quiberon Bay the Royal Navy destroyed the French fleet, so France could send no reserve. Montreal capitulated on 8 September 1760.
sections.sources:
Some of those present left accounts. Captain John Knox of the 43rd Foot wrote in his journal of the British volley and of the cry that the French were running as Wolfe lay dying. Dr Robert Macpherson of the 78th Highlanders wrote three days after the battle that the Highlanders pursued the French to the Sally Port of the town and then suffered heavy losses against Canadians in a village and a wood. Wolfe's last letter, dated HMS Sutherland, 8:30 p.m. on 12 September, and Brigadier-General George Townshend's remark that the general had changed his landing place on some intelligence also survive. Francis Parkman told the story in Montcalm and Wolfe. In 2017 a cannonball believed to have been fired during the siege was found in the Old City.

Much is uncertain. Totals for both armies vary between sources, and the number of French guns is not known. It is not known why Wolfe chose Foulon, when the original landing site was further upriver. Wolfe's disdain for his brigadiers and the effects of his illness and opiates have been suggested as influences, and some revisionist historians believe he expected the advanced guard to be repulsed and hoped to die gallantly. Montcalm's decision to attack at once has been regarded as precipitate, since he might have waited for Bougainville, avoided battle or yielded the city.
sections.legacy:
The battle proved a deciding moment in the conflict between France and Britain over the fate of New France, influencing the history of Canada. The capture of Quebec became part of what Britain called the Annus Mirabilis of 1759. The charge of the 78th Highlanders has been called the last known successful Highland Charge in history.

The war ended with the Treaty of Paris of 1763, which gave Britain parts of New France, including Canada and the eastern half of French Louisiana between the Mississippi River and the Appalachian Mountains.

In 2009 a planned re-enactment of the battle for its 250th anniversary was cancelled after threats of public disorder; leaders of separatist parties had called it a slap in the face for Quebecers of French ancestry. The Moulin à paroles, a recital of 140 texts from Quebec history on the Plains, went ahead without incident, though including the 1970 FLQ Manifesto brought a boycott by federalist politicians. A myth has Wolfe singing 'How Stands the Glass Around' the night before; Parkman says he recited Gray's Elegy.

summary: On 13 September 1759 British troops under James Wolfe, who had climbed to the Plains of Abraham by night, beat the French and Canadian force of the Marquis de Montcalm in about an hour. Both generals died, Quebec capitulated on 18 September, and France ceded Canada in 1763.

notes: Strengths: the article gives 4,426 British (Charbonneau, Government of Canada) against '7,700 troops' and 3,300 in the horseshoe; French 2,000+600+1,800 (Charbonneau) against about 3,500 in the attack and 13,390 available. I gave all of them with their attributions and did not reconcile them.

The article's 'Order of battle' lists the 48th as reserve and light infantry at the rear; the article's 'Main engagement' says Wolfe stood with the 28th and Grenadiers. The article says 'two battalions deployed facing north' and 'two in reserve' in the Battle text, while the order of battle shows one reserve regiment; I used the order of battle.
The article says the 78th took the highest casualties and was 'notably the last known successful Highland Charge'; the 'notably' wording is the article's.
The 'Overview' text mentions the 1758 Carillon, Louisbourg and Fort Frontenac events; left out for length.

The article contradicts itself on the French regiment relocation and the officer who could not patrol (no figures); not used. Its description of the 78th pursuit ('Sally Port') is from Macpherson's letter.

Left out: Wolfe's quoted letters to his mother, Vaudreuil's quotation, Montcalm's 'Not supposed that enemies have wings' remark, Wolfe's last words and Montcalm's, the French fire ships, and the Knox quotation in full.
Not in the article: Wolfe's age, any account of civilian deaths in Quebec's bombardment beyond the lower town being 'nearly levelled'.
